title: Capacity Sentinel: tiling, fencing, and soft-burst controls (PRD - WIP)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working PRD for Capacity Sentinel — a combined set of controls and runtime behaviors for Dedicated capacity that:
- prevents noisy-tenant impact via fencing and lightweight QoS lanes
- enables predictable short-term scaling (soft-burst credits + tile tiling)
- provides graceful degradation and automated failover into lower-cost model variants when capacity is constrained

Context and motivation:
We continue to see two types of production pain on Dedicated pools: (1) sudden microburst demand from a single tenant that either starves co-tenants or forces broad autoscale (high cost), and (2) poor isolation of traffic mixes (very low-latency chat vs long-running generation) leading to latency SLO violations. Current reserved-capacity and hard quota primitives are blunt instruments — they either block legitimate peaks or cause expensive overprovisioning. Capacity Sentinel aims to be the middle ground: a runtime + control-plane feature set that enforces tenant fencing, offers short-duration burst credit, and partitions pool resources into dynamically-allocated tiles for better isolation.

High level design principles:
- Safety first: default behavior should preserve SLOs for higher-tier tenants.
- Probabilistic fairness: avoid absolute hard caps unless explicitly configured.
- Transparent economics: customers can see how burst consumption maps to billing and credits.
- Operability: provide clear runbooks, observability, and one-click fallback actions for SREs.

Core concepts:
1) Tiles: logical slices of a GPU pool (not physical) that group request scheduling and KV-cache locality. Tiles make it cheaper to warm KV cache and reduce cross-tenant noise by preferring intra-tile scheduling for repeated requests. Each tile has configurable size (vCPU weight, GPU-slot count) and an affinity score tied to tenants.

2) Tenant Fencing: policy that prevents a tenant from spreading burst load across too many tiles concurrently. Fencing uses a token-per-tenant-per-tile mechanism; when a tenant exceeds concurrent tile tokens, additional requests are queued or routed to degraded model variants. Fencing is soft by default for self-serve plans; enterprise tenants can opt-in to strict fencing for isolation guarantees.

3) Burst Credits (microburst buffer): each tenant accrues short-term burst credits based on reserved capacity, historical steady-state traffic, and billing tier. Credits permit short duration (typically seconds to low minutes) above steady throughput without immediate eviction. Credits decay over time and are replenished with steady usage. Burst consumption is logged and surfaced with cost impact estimates.

4) Soft QoS Lanes: classify requests into lanes (hot/interactive, batch/long, embeddings) with lane-aware scheduling and separate proportional weight. Lanes can inherit different retry/backoff defaults and fallback models.

5) Degradation Policies: automated downgrade paths when a tenant hits hard limits or pool saturation:
- Route to a quantized/cheaper model variant with a short lived explanation header
- Throttle token rate with exponential backoff and explanatory request metadata
- Enqueue for next available tile (if latency SLOs permit)

API & Control plane surface:
- New route-level config fields: "tile_preference", "burst_policy" (mode: off|soft|strict), "burst_budget" (token count or seconds), "qos_lane_assignment"
- Admin API endpoints: /admin/tiles (inspect/resize), /admin/tenants/{id}/credits, /admin/tenants/{id}/fence-state
- Console: per-tenant burst burn rate, tile affinity heatmap, lane-level latency + CPU/GPU load charts

Autoscaling interaction:
- Autoscaler should be tile-aware. A pool scale action can either add tiles (preferred) or increase tile capacity.
- When tenants consume burst credits, autoscaler will consider both sustained and burst-adjusted load; autoscale triggers tied to short-window percentiles (p95 over 30s) and long-window baselines (p95 over 5m).
- To avoid oscillations: only scale out when long-window metrics also show elevated utilization or when aggregated burst consumption exceeds a threshold (configurable).

Operational runbook (initial):
- Detection: alert on sustained p99 latencies within a tile, burst-credit depletion events, and frequent fence-triggering (>50/min).
- Immediate mitigations: temporarily enable strict-fencing for offending tenant, initiate model downgrades, or route excess to Dedicated fallback lane (lower tier)
- Post-incident: run credit and tile-affinity audit; recommend changes to tenant burst budgets or propose reserved-capacity increase.

Observability and metrics (minimum):
- per-tenant: burst_credits_remaining, burst_credit_consumption_rate, fence_rejections, tile_affinity_score
- per-tile: active_tenants, queued_requests, p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU_utilization, KV_hit_rate
- pool-level: aggregate burst debt, tile fragmentation metric, autoscale_actions_count

Billing model proposal (brief):
- Burst window is free for very small bursts (e.g., first 10s per hour) to maintain product stickiness.
- Excess burst consumption billed as a separate line item with predictable unit (credit-second) and an associated discount for committed reserved capacity.
- Fine-grained telemetry is required for clear invoicing; surface predicted monthly cost impact in console.

UX/Console considerations:
- Clear indicators on route settings when a burst policy is active
- Tenant-facing dashboard showing current credits and historical burn (CSV export)
- Enable one-click recommended actions (increase burst budget, request more tiles, apply strict fencing) with ticket creation flow to Sales/CS for enterprise negotiations.

Rollout plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (internal dogfood): implement tiles and burst accounting in a single internal-only pool; no billing.
- Phase 1 (opt-in beta): expose soft-burst to dev/test tenants and select customers; collect telemetry and billing telemetry off by default.
- Phase 2 (self-serve): enable console controls and billing for burst; default soft policy for free tiers.
- Phase 3 (enterprise): strict-fencing and SLA-backed isolation options behind contract; integrate with Dedicated contracts and support playbooks.

Risks and mitigations:
- Complexity overhead: tiles and fencing add scheduling complexity. Mitigate by starting with coarse tiles and conservative defaults.
- Billing disputes: customers may be surprised by burst charges. Mitigate via generous free windows, explicit consent in console, and clear post-burn email notifications.
- Performance regression: enforcing fencing could increase tail latency for some tenants via queuing. Mitigate with canary and heavy telemetry, progressive rollout with opt-out.

Open questions / design decisions to resolve:
- Default tile size and heuristics for tile splitting/merging
- Exact credit accrual formula (static % of reservation vs usage-weighted)
- How to prioritize tenant affinity vs KV-cache warming benefits when scheduling across tiles
- Whether to allow cross-tenant preemption within a tile under emergency conditions (and what compensation looks like)

Next steps / immediate action items:
- Engineering spike: prototype tile scheduler and token fencing (owner: Diego Ramos, ETA: 3w)
- Billing: design credit-second pricing mockups and example invoices (owner: Lina Zhou, ETA: 2w)
- UX: console mockups for tile heatmaps and burst dashboard (owner: Omar Khan, ETA: 2w)
- SRE: draft emergency mitigation runbook and SLO changes (owner: SRE lead, ETA: 1w)

Notes to reviewers (informal):
- This doc is intentionally rough. Focus on whether the thin-slicing idea (tiles + burst credits + soft fencing) is compelling operationally and product-wise.
- If we like it, we should collapse a few of the closely-related existing PRDs into this single umbrella concept to reduce fragmentation.

End of draft.
